opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the core problem was that developers, and increasingly AI agents acting on behalf of developers, need a place to actually *run* things safely. Writing code is only half the loop. You want to execute it, see what happens, look at the data, iterate. Traditionally that meant either your laptop, which doesn't have access to the real data or the real compute, or a production cluster, where you really don't want someone experimenting freely.

So the vision for a sandbox is something in between: an isolated environment that spins up fast, has the right permissions and governance attached, can see the data you're allowed to see, and can't break anything it shouldn't. You should be able to throw it away when you're done, and nobody has to worry about what happened inside it.

What's changed recently is that the "user" of these sandboxes is often an agent. If you have a model generating code, you need to run thousands of these experiments, often in parallel, and you can't have a human reviewing every one before it executes. So isolation, fast startup, and good security boundaries become essential infrastructure rather than nice-to-haves. And you want the results to be observable, so you can trace what the agent did, why it did it, and whether the output was actually correct.

For me, a lot of it goes back to what we were trying to do with Spark and later the lakehouse: make it easy to bring compute to the data in a safe, governed way. Sandboxes are kind of the next step, making that interactive and cheap enough that you can experiment constantly, whether you're a person or a piece of software.

r001.rationale: The response describes sandboxes as fast to start and disposable (“throw it away when you're done”); it does not say they remain running instead of shutting down automatically.

r002.rationale: The response says developers need sandboxes to run code, inspect results, and iterate, and frames them as useful to both people and agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I've always thought about it, the sandbox isn't really the product. It's the thing that makes the product possible. When you look at what developers actually want, it's to go from an idea to something running, and to iterate on it quickly, without spending half their day on environment setup or worrying that they're going to break something.

So the vision was really a few things. First, isolation that's cheap enough that you don't have to think about it. If spinning up a clean environment takes seconds and costs almost nothing, you start using it everywhere: every test run, every experiment, every PR. That changes how you work, because you stop being precious about state. You can just try things.

Second, I wanted the sandbox to be where the data and the compute already are. A lot of what we did with Spark and later at Databricks was about that: you shouldn't have to copy data down to your laptop to explore it, and you shouldn't need a different mental model for "small thing on my machine" versus "big thing on the cluster." The sandbox should look like your local dev loop but be sitting right next to the data warehouse, the GPUs, whatever you need.

And then the third piece, which has become way more important with LLMs and agents, is that the sandbox is also where untrusted code runs. If you have a model generating code and executing it, you absolutely need a boundary around that. It's not just a convenience anymore, it's a safety property. So we've been thinking about sandboxes less as "a dev environment in the cloud" and more as the execution substrate for both humans and agents, where you can snapshot, fork, roll back, and observe everything that happened.

The thing that surprised me is how much that last part has driven adoption. People came in thinking they wanted a notebook, and what they really needed was a safe, reproducible place to let something, whether that's a person or a model, go off and try stuff.

r001.rationale: The response discusses quickly starting clean sandboxes and using them for experiments, tests, and PRs, but it does not say they would remain running or avoid automatic shutdown.

r002.rationale: It describes sandboxes supporting developers’ work from idea to running software, including tests, experiments, and PRs, as well as supporting agent sessions.

astra-6.text: The way I thought about it was giving developers an isolated environment where they could run code and experiment without having to manage all the infrastructure themselves. You could spin something up, try an idea, and throw it away when you were done. And because it’s in the cloud, you could make those environments reproducible and easy to share. The goal was to shorten that loop between having an idea and actually seeing it work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says environments could be thrown away when finished; it does not say they would remain running rather than shut down automatically.
